strings.GUZ_THENEWORDER_DESC: As with so many other provinces in the new China, Guizhou had been overrun by the Japanese forces and handed over to Chinese administration. He Yingqin soon found that his only 'army' was little more than an extension of Yunnan's clique of officers. During the 1950's He chose to focus on domestic development and building up the people's confidence in government once again. At every turn however he confronted with monopolists, Yunnan officers and the peoples own memory of the KMT's many failures. By 1960 it seemed He had turned reclusive, seemingly overcome by the many failures both of himself and the KMT he had loved. However, in meetings behind closed doors and in He Yingqin's personal audience a bold reform plan has been developed. Perhaps there is still hope for democracy in China after all...
strings.GUZ_paternalism_party_long: Southwestern Factions of the Nationalist Party of China
strings.GUZ_army_of_the_southwest_desc: While our civilian administration is fairly autonomous within the sphere, the control over our armed forces lies entirely within the hands of Lu Han, governor of Yunnan province. As such, we have no means to maintain our own military.
strings.GUZ_fascism_party_long: Nanjing Factions of the Nationalist Party of China
strings.GUZ_conservatism_DEF: Seventh Military Region of the NRA
strings.GUZ_Li_Pinxian_hog_desc: Li Pinxian was never supposed to be anyone in the Gui Clique. A Hunnan warlord seeking refuge in Guangxi, he was first and foremost an outsider to the Liangguang. If it wasn't for Huang Qixiang's public criticism of Li Zongren's actions that led to his eventual downfall, he would be likely to remain as a general than a supreme leader, and yet here he is. Taking over the legacy of Li Zongren, Pinxian climbed all the way to the position of vice-chairman of the Xinan Political Commission. As the first Gui leader to visit Kunming since the feud between the factions, it is assumed that he would play the role of a negotiator, softening up with the Dian Clique and changing the Isolationism of Li Zongren. After all, since Long Yun's days are numbered, it could be helpful to Yunnan-Guangxi relations in the future, perhaps even allowing the two to regain their old strength and rival that of Nanjing. For now, though, these remain but rumours, rumours that are yet to be confirmed.
strings.GUZ_Yang_Ruxuan_for_desc: When Yang Ruxuan returned to Kunming, he was no longer a follower of Zhu Peide. After the fall of Chongqing, seeing all hopes are lost, he is amongst the first batch of officers to surrender, and as a perk, were given extraordinary payment and status by the Japanese. Thus General Yang remained, staying in the General Staff of the Nanjing Regime. Since the Second Yun-Gui War, he has been dispatched by the Central Government to Kunming, taking part in the Japan-mediated peace talks, and was eventually left in Kunming to oversee many things here in the Southwest, as a liaison. In addition, he was also awarded many merely ceremonious roles, such as the Commandant of the Anti-Air forces. As it is part of his duty, he often excuses himself from the messy political scene and makes for the airports, where he spends hours each day, staring into the old landing strips, lost in thoughts.
strings.GUZ_Miao_Yuntai_eco_desc: A well-known industrialist, Miao Yuntai found the New Fudian Bank and for a long while had an almost complete monopoly of the Southwestern economy, even before he participated in the political scene. Years after Zhou Fohai purposely ruined his master project of transforming Yunnan, Miao Yuntai is now once more taking up the mantle of rejuvenating Yunnan and the entire Southwest. However, this time, rather than brilliant economic investments and austerities, Miao was forced to take a far more sinister path. Seeing Yunnan would otherwise fall into complete anarchy, Miao opted for more unconventional methods of acquiring funds and keeping the Three Provinces running. Since 1952, with the unofficial approval of Miao, the Yunnanese Army started production of opium, and its monopoly through rifles worked great to benefit the army and Miao Family. Now, Miao Yuntai has ascended to become the third most powerful player in the Southwest. What this 'Patriotic Capitalist' thinks of himself are not certain, but hatred towards him is well heard in every corner of the Southwest.
strings.GUZ_Lu_Han_sec_desc:
Lu Han has always been one of the closest companions of Chairman Long Yun and has always been the Second-in-Charge of the New Dian Clique essentially since its birth. Since He was expelled, the military affairs of Yunnan are now his alone to bear. As an old friend of Long, he is well aware of Long's great anguish, seeing how Yunnan, the Southwest, and the whole of China have become. As he ages, Long, ever more dull and senile, chose to bar himself from daily routines, and have grown numb. Every day, while taking over some of Long's work, he would pass by Long Yun's garden en route to picking up documents to look over and sign. And there he would see the old Marshal Long, sitting on a simple bench beneath a statue of him. His eyes idle and his thoughts far, all while his son ceaselessly bombards him with plans after plans, all of which unsettling to Lu. Lu Han knows when the day comes, he will be as immovable as his friendship with Chairman Long.

He must save Yunnan, and Long Yun.
strings.GUZ_what_china_desc: The Xinan Political Commission is a special entity within the Sphere indeed. Unlike the regimes of Sheng Shicai and Shi Yousan, the Xinan Commission does not need Japan's aid at all. Rather, it is Xinan who has been trading vital resources to Guangdong ever since its creation. Tokyo and Nanjing barely care if it sends its tribute, nor who controls the army. From an outside perspective, compared to most other regimes, Long Yun's Xinan has always been playing the role of an Anti-Japanese China within the Japanophile Sinosphere, but few know what would become a Post-Long Yun Southwest.
strings.GUZ_legacy_of_dianbi_desc:
In 1948, Zhou Fohai gave the Fudian Bank mintage rights. However, on top of that, he also lent a significant amount of old fiat currency created by the Chongqing Central Bank to Fudian. In a false sense of security, the Fudian engaged in large-scale money lending, leading to a high rate of non-performing accounts.

This escalated when in 1950, Zhou Fohai, under the pretext of unifying currency, made a demand to Fudian to immediately pay back all old fiat currency loans in exchange for the newer fiat currency, the Fabi issued by the Nanjing Central Bank. Needless to say, this completely broke the flow of money, and the Fudian Bank almost instantaneously declared bankruptcy.

As both Tokyo and Nanjing refused to lend out any more money on a significant scale, the Dianbi, or the Yunnan currency quickly devalued into nothing but play money. Many reconstructions and investment projects halted, and the Southwestern economy crashed. Although Long Yun stabilised it eventually by extending mintage to powerful bankers and merchant families, the damage was done. Yunnan's economy is in shambles, and there is little chance this situation would be changed.
strings.GUZ_legacy_of_the_third_diangui_war: Legacy of the Third Dian-Gui War
strings.GUZ_legacy_of_the_third_diangui_war_desc: In 1951, immediately after He's expulsion, Long Yun was deeply offended by Li Zongren's idea of inviting the Central Bank into the Southwest. Li, on the other hand, was also angered by his fierce regionalism and radical anti-Japanese behavior. But the foremost factor that drove the two factions to all-out war is perhaps their long-standing feud. Initially, the Dian Army, well known for being a force to reckon with, defeated advancing columns of Li and was making a dash for Baise. However, Japan's sudden entrance into the scene forced the two parties into peace by promising more autonomy. After the war, the Southwest on the surface is dominated by the Dian Clique, yet Guangxi won relatively autonomy in its military and financial affairs also, starting the decade-long internal strife between the two powerful cliques, eager to win the Southwest for themselves.
strings.GUZ_made_in_xinan_desc:
After the Dianbi Catastrophe, the Xinan Political Commission was forced to seek funds elsewhere, eventually reaching out to some dubious loan sharks based in Europe, their identity unknown and their money mysterious. To pay back debt as soon as possible without incurring huge interest, the Xinan regime was forced to resort to Opium cultivation, the production of which allowed Xinan to smoothly exit the monetary crisis, and helped pull its citizens out of poverty.

Although strict policies in the Southwest prevented a humanitarian crisis of opium addiction (And that most Chinese, due to the Opium Wars, largely despised drug consumption), drugs nonetheless took over as a main source of income, as capitalists rush to these highlight valuable industries, abandoning others to eventual bankruptcy. Yunnan, who was hit the hardest, was the biggest offender, investing openly in drug production. As history enters the 1960s, Xinan is capable of producing many dozen types of drugs, including LSDs and Heroins, Southwestern made drugs are now sold worldwide, even more than the rice grains of China and electronics of Guangdong.
strings.GUZ_mountains_of_madness_desc: After the Dianbi Catastrophe, Chairman He Yingqin was expelled in a coup from Kunming into the mountains of Guizhou where he originated from, alongside some of the better-equipped forces of Xinan, forming the Neo Xingyi Clique by allying himself with the remnants of Xingyi Clique warlords. At the same time, Yang Sen, who is also exiled from his lands amidst Sichuanese civil wars also went into hiding with Guizhou alongside his ragtag 20th Army, forging an alliance with the nominal chairman of the province Wang Jialie, forming what is called the Tongzi Clique. And thus, the battle of the three armies ensued in Guizhou for decades, in one of the poorest, smallest, and least developed provinces of all China.
strings.GUZ_a_new_industry_desc:
The Southwest grew, but only a few tasted the fruits. Outside of major cities and towns, warlord infighting and breach of drug laws led to a significant decline of labour force in the rural areas, driving the peasantry in the Southwest into extreme poverty. And out of desperation, an industry arguably eviler than drug trafficking was born.

Human trafficking has been common, but not to the point of being widespread ever since the term China was coined. Although the central government back in the 1920s actively suppressed it, many villagers in the Southwest, now with nothing to sell, are now selling their daughters and spare women to the faraway central plains of China. Some families thought they were giving the female in question a better chance to live a decent life from rumours about Nanjing and its richness, but most had not the time to think about such things. Meanwhile, some trafficking groups, blacked by officials through bribes are also known to forcibly kidnap women and female students of the urban areas, who are sold at higher prices for being 'educated'. Terrorising the women of Kunming and Dali to the point that few if none dare to travel by themselves unless armed.

Under the watchful eyes of the statues of Long Yun, human trafficking is an organised, efficient and effective industry.
